summary: Trabectedin (YONDELIS) is an intravenous alkylating agent indicated for unresectable or metastatic liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma in patients who have received a prior anthracycline-containing regimen. It is given as 1.5 mg/m2 by 24-hour IV infusion through a central venous line every 21 days, with dexamethasone 20 mg IV premedication. Trabectedin carries multiple serious warnings: neutropenic sepsis and serious neutropenia, rhabdomyolysis (with potential for fatal muscle and renal injury), hepatotoxicity including hepatic failure, cardiomyopathy with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, and severe tissue necrosis from extravasation - which is why it must be administered through a central venous line. Treatment requires baseline and ongoing monitoring of blood counts, liver chemistries, creatine phosphokinase (CPK), and cardiac function, with dose modification or discontinuation for these toxicities.
indications: Unresectable or metastatic liposarcoma in adults who have received a prior anthracycline-containing regimen
Unresectable or metastatic leiomyosarcoma in adults who have received a prior anthracycline-containing regimen

dosage.d: 1.5 mg/m2 as a continuous intravenous infusion over 24 hours, repeated every 21 days, until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity
dosage.n: Administer through a central venous line; premedicate with dexamethasone 20 mg IV 30 minutes prior

dosage.d: Dexamethasone 20 mg IV 30 minutes before each trabectedin dose
Reduce to 1.2 mg/m2, then 1.0 mg/m2 for severe neutropenia, hepatic, muscle, or cardiac toxicity; do not re-escalate after a reduction
dosage.n: Permanently discontinue for persistent or severe toxicity per label

dosage.d: Reduce starting dose to 0.9 mg/m2 every 21 days (moderate impairment); do not initiate if bilirubin is above normal
dosage.n: Avoid in severe hepatic impairment (not studied)

admin: Administer ONLY through a central venous line - extravasation can cause severe tissue necrosis; a peripheral line is not appropriate
Premedicate with dexamethasone 20 mg IV 30 minutes before each dose
Reconstitute and dilute per labeling; give as a continuous 24-hour intravenous infusion using an in-line 0.2 micron filter
Do not initiate a cycle until neutrophils are at least 1500/mcL, platelets at least 100,000/mcL, and bilirubin, transaminases/alkaline phosphatase, and CPK meet label thresholds
Handle as a hazardous cytotoxic agent; if extravasation is suspected stop the infusion immediately and manage the site
moa: Trabectedin is an alkylating drug that binds guanine residues in the minor groove of DNA, forming adducts and bending the DNA helix toward the major groove. This binding affects multiple transcription factors, DNA-binding proteins, and DNA repair pathways, resulting in perturbation of the cell cycle. It interferes with transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair, leading to the formation of lethal DNA strand breaks and ultimately apoptosis of tumor cells; sensitivity is partly dependent on a functional nucleotide excision repair system.

absolute: Do not initiate when total bilirubin is above the upper limit of normal (hepatotoxicity/hepatic failure risk)
relative: Elevated CPK or active muscle injury (rhabdomyolysis risk)
Pre-existing cardiac dysfunction or reduced LVEF (cardiomyopathy risk)
monitor: Complete blood counts (assess neutrophils before each dose and as needed) for neutropenic sepsis/neutropenia
Creatine phosphokinase (CPK) before each dose for rhabdomyolysis
Liver function tests and bilirubin before each dose and as indicated for hepatotoxicity/hepatic failure
Left ventricular ejection fraction (echocardiogram or MUGA) at baseline and periodically for cardiomyopathy; the infusion site for extravasation

preg: Based on its mechanism and animal data, trabectedin can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman. Advise pregnant women of the potential risk to the fetus. Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment and for 2 months after the last dose, and advise males with female partners to use condoms during and after treatment per labeling.
lact: There are no data on the presence of trabectedin in human milk or its effects on the breastfed child or milk production. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a breastfed infant, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment and for a period (e.g., several days) after the final dose.
renal: No dosage adjustment is needed for mild to moderate renal impairment (creatinine clearance 30-89 mL/min). Trabectedin has not been studied in severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min) or end-stage renal disease; use is not recommended in these populations. Maintain adequate hydration given rhabdomyolysis risk.
hepatic: Trabectedin causes hepatotoxicity, including cases of hepatic failure. Do not initiate trabectedin in patients with a total bilirubin above the upper limit of normal. Assess liver chemistries (bilirubin, transaminases, alkaline phosphatase) before each dose and as clinically indicated, and manage elevations with dose interruption, reduction, or discontinuation per labeling. For patients with moderate hepatic impairment, reduce the starting dose; avoid use in severe hepatic impairment because it has not been studied. Dexamethasone premedication reduces hepatotoxicity.

major: Strong CYP3A inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole) - increase trabectedin exposure and toxicity; avoid concomitant use
Strong CYP3A inducers (e.g., rifampin) - decrease trabectedin exposure/efficacy; avoid concomitant use
Other hepatotoxic drugs - additive risk of liver injury/hepatic failure
moderate: Drugs causing myelosuppression - additive neutropenia and infection risk
Statins and other myotoxic agents - may add to rhabdomyolysis risk; monitor CPK
Cardiotoxic agents (including cumulative anthracyclines) - additive cardiomyopathy risk
minor: No clinically significant minor interactions specifically documented
interactions.food: Not applicable; trabectedin is administered intravenously, not orally. Avoid grapefruit (a CYP3A inhibitor).
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol because of additive hepatotoxicity risk.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor CBC, liver chemistries with bilirubin, creatine phosphokinase (CPK), and left ventricular ejection fraction.

serious: Neutropenic sepsis and serious/severe neutropenia (including fatal)
Rhabdomyolysis (with potential for fatal muscle injury and acute renal failure)
Cardiomyopathy with decreased left ventricular ejection fraction and heart failure
Extravasation causing severe tissue necrosis requiring debridement

monitoring: Complete blood counts before each dose and as needed during the cycle; assess for fever/neutropenic sepsis and hold or reduce dose for severe neutropenia
Creatine phosphokinase (CPK) before each dose; if CPK rises or rhabdomyolysis is suspected, withhold and discontinue as indicated and provide supportive care
Liver function tests and total bilirubin before each dose; do not initiate if bilirubin is elevated and manage hepatotoxicity by interruption/reduction/discontinuation
Left ventricular ejection fraction by echocardiogram or MUGA at baseline and periodically; withhold/discontinue for cardiomyopathy or symptomatic LV dysfunction
Inspect the central line and infusion site for extravasation throughout the 24-hour infusion
counsel: This medicine is given through a central line over 24 hours every 3 weeks, with a steroid (dexamethasone) before each dose
Report fever or signs of infection immediately - low white cells with infection can be life-threatening
Report muscle pain, weakness, or dark/cola-colored urine right away (muscle breakdown), and any yellowing of skin or eyes (liver injury)
Report shortness of breath, swelling, or a racing/irregular heartbeat (possible heart effects); tell your team of any pain, redness, or swelling at the infusion site
Avoid pregnancy and breastfeeding; use effective contraception during and after treatment, and avoid alcohol
pk: Antitumor effect over treatment cycles; given as a 24-hour continuous infusion
Steady-state concentrations approached during the 24-hour infusion
Terminal half-life approximately 175 hours (long, due to extensive tissue distribution)
Dosed every 21 days; prolonged distribution and elimination
Store unopened vials refrigerated at 2-8 C; protect from light; use reconstituted/diluted solution within labeled time limits
pearls: Multiple serious warnings: neutropenic sepsis/neutropenia, rhabdomyolysis, hepatotoxicity/hepatic failure, cardiomyopathy, and extravasation necrosis - monitor CBC, CPK, LFTs/bilirubin, and LVEF
Must be given through a CENTRAL venous line over 24 hours - peripheral extravasation causes severe tissue necrosis
Always premedicate with dexamethasone 20 mg IV; it reduces hepatotoxicity and nausea
Do not initiate a cycle if bilirubin is above ULN, neutrophils <1500/mcL, platelets <100,000/mcL, or CPK exceeds the label threshold
Avoid strong CYP3A inhibitors and inducers; reduce starting dose in moderate hepatic impairment and avoid in severe impairment
missed: Trabectedin is administered on a 21-day cycle by the oncology team. A dose is delayed (not skipped) until blood counts, liver chemistries, and CPK recover to labeled thresholds; cycles may be extended up to about 3 weeks beyond schedule to allow recovery, and the dose is reduced if recovery is delayed or toxicity occurred. If a planned cycle is missed, the treating team reschedules it after confirming recovery rather than giving a double dose. Do not re-escalate the dose after a reduction.
overdose: There is no specific antidote for trabectedin overdose. Overdosage would be expected to intensify adverse effects, particularly myelosuppression (neutropenic sepsis), hepatotoxicity, rhabdomyolysis, and gastrointestinal toxicity. Management is supportive, including close monitoring and treatment of cytopenias (transfusions, growth factors, infection control), liver and muscle/renal function, and other organ toxicities until recovery.
